title: Attachment Styles and Partner Control
abstract: Past research in relationship science has found a link between engagement in the Michelangelo phenomenon, supporting one’s romantic partner’s desires to become their ideal self, to more positive relationship outcomes. In contrast, past research has also found that engagement in the Pygmalion phenomenon, characterized by an individual pushing one’s romantic partner into becoming who they want their partner to become, has been linked to adverse relationship outcomes. Study 1 investigated whether there is a potential link between insecure adult attachment styles and engagement in the Pygmalion phenomenon. Results indicated that levels of avoidant attachment, but not anxious attachment, were significantly associated with the more controlling and less supportive Pygmalion phenomenon. Study 2 attempted to examine possible mechanisms through which avoidant attachment was uniquely associated with engaging in the Pygmalion phenomenon. Two competing hypotheses were tested. The primary hypothesis was that this association emerged from avoidantly attached individuals misperceiving their own partner as controlling, and responding with controlling behaviors (i.e., engaging in the Pygmalion phenomenon). A secondary hypothesis was that the association was due to a previously documented association between avoidant attachment and Machiavellianism. Although the initial findings of Study 1 did not replicate in Study 2, results from mediation analyses did indicate that Machiavellianism, and not a misperception of control, served as an indirect link for avoidance with Pygmalion behaviors. In other words, avoidantly attached individuals who are particularly Machiavellian may be the ones who are most likely to engage in Pygmalion behaviors.
